extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, appellate practitioners, judges, and legal policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of the federal "administrative-remand rule": its definition, origins, circuit variations, problems, systemic effects, and recommended reforms for appeals of agency remands under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative-remand rule (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An order remanding an administrative agency’s decision under the federal Administrative Procedure Act is final only as to the agency; only the agency may appeal a remand, and if the agency does not appeal, neither the plaintiff nor any intervenor may do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as an appellate gatekeeper in almost all cases involving remands to federal agencies and thus shapes much of the administrative law developed in the courts of appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: promote judicial economy / avoid piecemeal appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule emerged in the 1970s and 1980s to promote judicial economy by avoiding piecemeal appeals, even at the cost of injustice in particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the avoidance of piecemeal appeals and judicial efficiency as the primary historical justification for the rule; recognize the trade-off between efficiency and potential injustice to individual parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit variation and inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: All the federal circuits have adopted the rule, but very different versions of it. A non-agency party’s ability to appeal a remand varies significantly from circuit to circuit and, in some cases, even within the same circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how divergences among circuits create unpredictability and may warrant harmonizing adjustments; pay attention to intra-circuit doctrinal splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic category — remand likely to be meaningless
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule is problematic in cases where a remand is likely to be meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When remand will not materially change the outcome or only delays resolution without substantive change, consider permitting non-agency appeals to avoid hollow procedures and unnecessary delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic category — remand facilitates ongoing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule is problematic where it facilitates ongoing harm to parties or resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If remand prolongs or perpetuates harm (to parties, rights, or resources), that practical injustice is a ground for limiting the gatekeeping effect of the rule and allowing appellate review by non-agency parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule as appellate gatekeeper and its effects on administrative law
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative-remand rule acts as an appellate gatekeeper in almost all cases involving remands to federal agencies and accordingly shapes much of the administrative law coming out of the federal courts of appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess doctrinal developments and precedent selection with awareness that the rule filters which issues reach the courts of appeals and thereby influences substantive administrative-law doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader systemic concerns raised by the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule underscores larger concerns, including forum-shopping, temporal forum-shopping, politicized agency decision-making, inconsistent judicial review, and reduced access to the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these systemic pathologies when evaluating the desirability of the rule or of particular applications: does the rule enable strategic forum selection, timing-based manipulation, politicization of agency responses, uneven review, or barriers to court access?

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and deference considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule reveals much about how the courts of appeals conceive of finality and deference to agency decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how notions of finality and doctrines of judicial deference (e.g., respect for agency processes) inform where courts draw the line on appealability after remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended reform criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Modest adjustments should make the administrative-remand rule more consistent across the circuits, better balance judicial efficiency and justice, and promote better agency decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three goals (consistency, balance of efficiency and fairness, and incentives for better agency decision-making) as evaluative criteria when proposing or assessing reforms to the rule.
